newsitem.title: USA: Dole preaches trust and tax cuts in Michigan.
newsitem.headline: Dole preaches trust and tax cuts in Michigan.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole took his message of trust and tax cuts to the must-win state of Michigan on Monday, trying to slice President Bill Clinton's commanding lead in the polls.

On a bus tour through colourful foliage and picturesque small towns of this key state, Dole promised voters his 15 percent federal income tax cut would spur the U.S. economy and painted Clinton as a slippery liberal they cannot trust.

Dole charged that Clinton was taking credit for millions of new jobs he did not create. "He (Clinton) has a way of walking right over the facts and looking you in the eye and telling you something that didn't happen," he said.

Michigan is a swing state that is part of a bloc of Midwestern states analysts say Dole must win to offset Clinton's advantage in the most populous states. But with only 15 days until the election and a yawning gap in national and state polls, Dole faces an uphill battle.

The latest Reuters daily tracking poll released on Monday showed Clinton had regained a double-digit lead over Dole, leading the Republican by 46.6 to 35.8 percent. The poll, conducted by John Zogby Group International, showed that Dole's upsurge following the second presidential debate last week was brief and Clinton was again stretching his lead.

The Kansas Republican seemed almost wistful at times, wondering at an economic forum in Detroit why people had turned off his last debate with Clinton and seemed to be tuning out the campaign in general.

"The election is about two weeks from now and a lot of people haven't focused," Dole said."Maybe there's no interest in politics, maybe nobody cares or maybe they're just getting around to focus on it and they're making up their minds."
At a rally in the small town of Chelsea, in what should be a Republican part of the state, he said he did not understand how Clinton had managed to connect with voters there.

There were a number of pro-Clinton signs in the crowd and one person held up sign in which Dole's 15 percent tax cut slogan had been altered to read "15 percent behind." The local high school band played the theme from "Mission Impossible."

Michigan Republican Gov. John Engler, travelling with Dole, told reporters he believed the former senator could manage a narrow win. But Wisconsin Republican Gov. Tommy Thompson, absent from a Monday morning forum with Dole and Republican governors in Detroit, has publicly criticised Dole's campaign as mismanaged.
"Tommy is very outspoken, that's a Wisconsin trait I guess," Engler told reporters.

In Detroit, Dole and the governors charged that Clinton was unfairly taking credit for an improved economy, claiming the rosier outlook was largely due to tax cuts and often painful economic reforms pushed through at the state level.

The complaints reflected frustration that Dole's economic plan, the centrepiece of his campaign, has not sold well. Polls have shown many voters are sceptical about Dole's vow to both cut taxes and balance the budget.

Dole, who called on Sunday for banning all campaign contributions from non-U.S. citizens, again criticised Democrats for questionable donations from individuals with ties to an Indonesian financial conglomerate.
